title: Integumentary system: skin, hair and nails
note: The skin has a Greek root (derm/o, dermat/o) and a Latin one (cutane/o). Hair is pil/o or trich/o, and nail is onych/o or ungu/o. Color roots appear across the body: erythr/o red, leuk/o white, melan/o black, cyan/o blue, xanth/o yellow.

read.title: Reading the skin
text: The integumentary system is the skin together with the hair, nails, and the sweat and oil glands. Its outer layer, the epidermis, is built mainly of cells filled with keratin, a tough protein, which is why kerat/o means hard or horny tissue in skin terms. Pigment cells in the epidermis, the melanocytes, make the dark pigment melanin. Beneath lies the dermis, which carries blood vessels, nerves, glands and hair follicles, and below that a subcutaneous layer of fat.

Skin vocabulary rewards learning a few small sets. Each structure has two roots, one Greek and one Latin: derm/o and cutane/o for skin, trich/o and pil/o for hair, onych/o and ungu/o for nail. Glands are named by what they release: hidr/o is sweat and seb/o is sebum, the oil that keeps skin and hair supple.

Color roots are also worth knowing early because they recur in every system. Erythr/o is red, leuk/o white, melan/o black, cyan/o blue and xanth/o yellow. Combine them with suffixes you already know and many terms decode themselves: cyanosis is an abnormal bluish color, and xeroderma is dry skin.
